newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil business community in mourning after crash.
newsitem.headline: Brazil business community in mourning after crash.

text.p: Brazil's financial community was in mourning on Friday, trying to overcome the shock of a tragic air disaster that took the lives of dozens of the country's business executives.

TAM Flight 402, which crashed into a densely populated Sao Paulo neighbourhood soon after takeoff on Thursday, was carrying 96 passengers and crew bound for Rio de Janeiro. Most were bankers and executives from top Brazilian and international companies headed to Rio for morning meetings.

"It could have been any one of us on that plane. I have made the trip a thousand times. That is why all the financial markets were so affected by this," said an economist at a Brazilian bank who asked not to be identified.
Thousands of business executives make the routine commute each week between Brazil's two main financial centres, much like their counterparts in Los Angeles and San Francisco or New York and Boston.
Leading retail bank Unibanco lost eight officials in various departments, slowing the bank's trading operations to a quarter of its normal activity.
Coca-Cola, Citibank, Bank of Boston, Chase, Siemens, Parmalat, Hoescht, Boehringer and Asea Brown Boveri were among the multinational firms with executives on board Flight 402.

News of the accident froze trading on the Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro stock markets, where traders put down their pencils and tickets to learn more about the fatal flight, which killed all 96 on board and at least eight on the ground.

Trading volume on Sao Paulo's stock exchange on Thursday was down nearly 50 percent. "This accident stopped the market. There were many people who lost colleagues in the crash and it took away any desire to work," a Sao Paulo trader said.

TAM, Latin America's fastest growing regional carrier, has attributed much of its success to building a niche among business clients by adapting flight times to meet the financial community's hectic schedules and offering an attractive frequent-flyer plan.
Veterans of the commute say it was the first accident between the two cities in more than 20 years.
Despite Thursday's tragedy, most in the financial community said the markets would return to normal next week.
"Business was certainly affected by this yesterday and today. I think next week we will get back to normal," said Caludio Haddad, chief executive officer at Brazilian investment bank Garantia.
